definition: Degumming removes gummy non-fiber material from a fiber: most often the sericin coating of silk, and also the pectins and hemicelluloses that bind ramie and other bast fibers.
explanation: Raw silk consists of paired fibroin filaments glued together and coated by sericin, a water-soluble, largely amorphous protein. Degumming dissolves that sericin, usually in hot or boiling aqueous baths with soap and sodium carbonate, or with enzymes, leaving the smooth fibroin that gives silk its luster, hand and drape. It can be done on yarn, or on fabric woven 'in the gum'. For ramie, decorticated ribbons are boiled in alkaline solutions to strip plant gums and separate the fibers, a step with the same purpose but different chemistry.
example: A weaver buys raw silk yarn that feels stiff and slightly harsh. After a sample skein is simmered in a soap and soda bath, it loses about a quarter of its weight and becomes softer, brighter and more supple. Because the loss is mostly sericin, a buyer comparing prices needs to know whether a silk's weight is quoted before or after degumming.
caution: Partial degumming can be intentional, leaving some sericin for body, as in souple silks. Over-degumming, prolonged boiling or strong alkali damages fibroin, lowering strength and encouraging fibrillation. Degumming loss is different from weight added later by dyeing or by weighting with metal salts. For bast fibers the word refers to removing plant polysaccharides, not protein.
deeper: Studies using sodium carbonate report degumming losses of about 25 to 26 percent of raw silk mass, and borate buffers about 27 percent, consistent with sericin forming roughly a quarter of cocoon silk. A common laboratory protocol boils silk in 0.02 M sodium carbonate for 30 to 60 minutes and then rinses repeatedly, and is widely used to prepare fibroin for biomaterials. Alkaline treatment also hydrolyzes and shortens fibroin chains, so gentler routes are studied: the protease papain preserves higher fibroin molecular weight, and high-temperature, high-pressure water can separate sericin without added chemicals. The moth's own protease, cocoonase, which softens the cocoon at emergence, has also been studied for degumming.
origins: The English term reflects the long-standing description of sericin as silk 'gum', although chemically it is a protein rather than a plant gum. The word was later applied to bast fiber processing, where true plant gums (pectins and hemicelluloses) are removed. Hot-water and soap treatments of silk long predate modern chemistry, while enzyme and high-pressure methods are recent research directions aimed at gentler, lower-chemical processing.

definition: A disperse dye is a small, nonionic, sparingly water-soluble colorant applied as a fine aqueous dispersion that dissolves into hydrophobic fibers, chiefly polyester.
explanation: Polyester has no ionic sites and is too hydrophobic for water-soluble dyes. Disperse dyes are milled into fine particles and held in suspension by dispersing agents; a small fraction dissolves in the bath, diffuses into the fiber's amorphous regions and remains there as a solid solution. Uptake is slow at the boil because polyester chains are tightly packed, so polyester is usually dyed in pressurized machines above 100 C. Disperse dyes also color nylon, acetate and similar hydrophobic fibers.
example: A lab dyes the same polyester fabric twice with one disperse dye, once at 100 C and once at 130 C in a pressurized vessel. The 130 C sample is noticeably deeper. After a hot-press test, the lighter sample shows little change, but a deep navy sample may mark an adjacent white fabric, showing why sublimation fastness is checked for polyester.
caution: Disperse dyes cannot color cotton meaningfully, so polyester-cotton blends need a second dye class for the cotton. Some disperse dyes are recognized contact allergens, and textile dye mixes appear in dermatological patch testing. Deep shades can migrate or sublime during heat setting, pressing or storage. Good wash results do not guarantee good sublimation or light fastness.
deeper: Dyeing proceeds by dissolution of dye molecules from particles, adsorption at the fiber surface and diffusion into the polymer, the rate-limiting step. Diffusion rises sharply once the polymer passes its glass transition and segmental motion opens free volume, which is why temperature dominates. Studies synthesizing new azo disperse dyes report clear gains in color strength when dyeing temperature rises from 100 C to 130 C, and high-temperature, high-pressure dyeing giving the highest K/S values compared with other methods. Fastness is assessed for washing, rubbing, light and sublimation using grey scale ratings. Chemically, many disperse dyes are azo or anthraquinone structures with polar substituents that tune shade and affinity. Patch-test studies list Disperse Blue 106 and 124 among allergens tested.
origins: Disperse dyes were developed for hydrophobic manufactured fibers that ionic dyes colored poorly, and their importance grew with polyester, which now accounts for a large share of fiber production. Modern research continues to design new disperse structures, dispersants and waterless or low-water application routes, including digital inkjet systems for polyester. Specific first-commercialization dates were not verified for this edition.

definition: Drafting attenuates a fiber strand by making fibers slide past one another, usually between pairs of rollers running at increasing surface speeds, so the strand becomes longer and finer.
explanation: A drafting zone grips the strand at two nips. The front, or delivery, rollers turn faster than the back, or feed, rollers, so each fiber released by the back nip is accelerated as soon as the front nip catches it. Drafting happens on drawframes, roving frames and ring frames, and on worsted gill boxes, where pinned fallers control fibers between the rollers. At the drawframe several slivers are fed together (doubling) while being drafted, which averages out irregularities; drafting also straightens fibers and aligns them with the strand axis.
example: A drawframe is fed six slivers of 5 ktex each, 30 ktex in total, and delivers one sliver of 5 ktex. The total draft is therefore 6, matching the ratio of delivery to feed roller surface speeds. The output is no finer than any single input sliver, but blending six sources into one makes it noticeably more even.
caution: Drafting is not twisting; twist is added afterward, or on a roving frame in the same machine, to consolidate the drafted strand. A higher draft is not automatically better, because fibers held by neither nip, called floating fibers, move irregularly and create thick and thin places. The spacing between nips relative to fiber length matters as much as the draft figure itself.
deeper: Draft is the ratio of delivery surface speed to feed surface speed and, ignoring waste, equals input linear density divided by output linear density. Total draft over several zones is the product of the zone drafts. In cotton spinning drafting systems, the back-zone break draft is usually about 1.1 to 1.5 and the front-zone main draft about 6 to 30. Aprons in the main zone guide fibers too short to span the nip distance. Nip spacing is set somewhat longer than the longest fibers, so no fiber is gripped by both nips at once, which would break it or make it slip erratically. On drawframes, a tension draft of slightly less than one is used between delivery and feed points to keep slivers taut without drafting them.
origins: Roller drafting was the central idea of the mechanized spinning machines of eighteenth-century England, replacing the hand spinner's fingers that drew fibers out of a distaff or rolag. The older English verb 'draw' survives in the names drawframe and drawing, while mill technicians use 'draft' for the numerical ratio of speeds. Wool worsted systems developed the pinned gill box to control long fibers during the same operation.
